g.text: Reliable streams over independent Mix messages
Applications read and write streams. MixTransport manages the messages underneath.
The same bytes, in the same order
Mix carries the messages through relays
One sending direction shown. The stream works in both directions.
MixTransport adds sessions, ordering, flow control and return capacity above Mix.
01 — Legacy connections and the message API
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / CONNECTIONS AND MESSAGES
Legacy connections and the message API
Legacy reply-expecting connections handle one request. MixTransport manages sessions and streams.
with a reference to this connection’s
ExitLayer takes it after the handler returns.
At B: ExitLayer sends the response
Reply returns through Mix; A recovers it.
If the destination is beyond the exit, the exit uses a regular libp2p connection instead of MixExitConnection.
The exit collects that reply using the codec’s response reader.
MixTransport: messages belong to sessions and streams
MixTransport supplies SURBs, retains reply credentials, and dispatches incoming frames.
Mix delivers messages through callbacks instead of an entry connection’s read queue.
Connection objects are local wrappers, not a regular libp2p connection.
In both modes, replies return via SURBs. At A, recovered bytes enter the requesting connection’s incoming queue.
02 — Reliable streams over independent Mix messages
04 — Session roles determine forward and reverse
Session roles determine forward and reverse
A is the session initiator. B is the session recipient and forward path's final Mix hop.
REVERSE · route supplied by a SURB
A knows how to address B.
B receives a return path, not A's network address.
Mix API: forward ⇒ send(...); reverse ⇒ sendWithSurb(...)
Forward/reverse describe session direction—not who opened a stream.
05 — One session ID, two local views
One session ID, two local views
A generates pseudonym S. Both endpoints use S in transport frames.
S is not a network address
B can reuse S for another stream, but cannot start a new session to an unknown A.
06 — Establish the session before opening streams
Establish the session before opening streams
Connect carries both the session ID and initial return capacity.
First 2 SURBs ⇒ ConnectAck copies. Remaining 3 ⇒ initial session queue.
Mix API: createSurb returns a SURB to transmit and a credential to retain locally.
Session establishment creates return capacity; an application stream comes next.
07 — Either endpoint can open a stream
Either endpoint can open a stream
Session roles stay fixed. Stream opener and acceptor roles depend on each opening.
A allocates odd IDs: 1, 3, 5… B allocates even IDs: 2, 4, 6…
Every established stream is bidirectional, regardless of its opener.
(sessionId, streamId) identifies a stream; each direction has its own Data sequence.
Sequence 7 on stream 2 is unrelated to sequence 7 on another stream or direction.
09 — Chunk application bytes into Data frames
Chunk application bytes into Data frames
Write boundaries are not preserved; the receiver reconstructs an ordered byte stream.
Current payload bound: 3,835 bytes. Each direction numbers chunks starting at 1.
Large writes become multiple frames; reads can cross the original write boundaries.
10 — Redundancy uses distinct SURBs for one frame
Redundancy uses distinct SURBs for one frame
A second copy increases delivery opportunities—not the number of application bytes.
Each SURB has its own credential identifier. Data de-duplication uses stream sequence state.
A later retry keeps sequence + payload, but uses fresh SURBs and a fresh supply snapshot.
Mix API: sendWithSurb at B; RawSurbReply callback + recoverReply at A. Default redundancy: 2.
SURB-identifier retirement and logical Data de-duplication are different mechanisms.
13 — The receive window holds out-of-order chunks
The receive window holds out-of-order chunks
Example: base = 4. Sequences 1–3 already entered the ordered buffer.
Receive window: 256 positions; only the first 8 are shown.
ACK: base 4; bitmap acknowledges 5 and 6. They cannot be delivered before 4.
After ordered-buffer admission: base advances to 7; the window moves.
Bitmap acknowledgements release retained sender copies.
Advancing the receive base allows the sender to send further sequence numbers.
14 — Slow readers eventually stop the sender
Slow readers eventually stop the sender
Backpressure propagates through bounded buffering and the receive window.
Two independent bounds: 256-position remote window + 64 retained chunks per direction.
An ACK means retained/deliverable bytes—not that the application has processed them.
Even fully bitmap-acknowledged chunks do not move a stalled receive base.
15 — One SURB queue serves all streams in a session
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / SHARED RETURN CAPACITY
One SURB queue serves all streams in a session
B uses accepted SURBs in arrival order; missing supply sequences do not block their use.
Reverse frame: take 2 SURBs from the front; never return spent entries.
Mix API: createSurb + serializeSurb at A; deserializeSurb + sendWithSurb at B.
Streams share return capacity. Dedicated response SURBs stay outside this queue.
18 — Spending two SURBs makes room for two more
Spending two SURBs makes room for two more
The received sequence numbers stay acknowledged, even after B spends their SURBs.
Example: B has received all numbered SURBs 0–15; its queue capacity is 16.
base = 16 bitmap = all zero bits limit = 16
base = 16 bitmap = all zero bits limit = 18
Base 16 already acknowledges 0–15. No SURBs numbered 16 or later have arrived.
In both rows, the bitmap describes sequences starting at 16.
None of those SURBs has arrived, so all bits are zero.
Spending two SURBs raises the limit from 16 to 18.
A may supply new SURBs 16 and 17; number 18 is still excluded.
A estimates inventory from available supply slots; it does not refill every small gap.
Low watermark = 11. At estimate 10, six free positions can be filled as packets of 5 + 1.
Count SURBs already allocated for delivery, even if they have not arrived yet,
20 — An empty queue can still answer a status probe
An empty queue can still answer a status probe
A supplies a fresh response path when reverse activity goes silent.
Reference policy: probe after 2 minutes of silence; up to 3 attempts, 30 seconds apart.
Continued silence after the final response interval ends the local session.
A valid reverse snapshot restores activity knowledge—even if B has no application data.
21 — Keep three kinds of state separate
Keep three kinds of state separate
One session ties them together; each answers a different question.
Session S + stream ID; opener roles can differ on each stream.
Per-direction Data sequences, ACK bitmap, receive window and retained chunks.
Session-wide SURB inventory, supply receipt bitmap, supply limit and reply credentials.
A lost receive-window update can leave a sender stalled;
the current protocol has no Data-window probe.
Mix supplies the message primitives; MixTransport supplies the communication model.
How a session is established, how its streams carry data, and how the recipient can send back.
identities, and paths in both directions.
and waiting for a slow reader.
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / RECEIVE WINDOW · PURPOSE
Mix messages can arrive out of order; the receiver must bound how far ahead it accepts Data.
A gap must not create an unlimited backlog.
Keep later chunks while waiting for the gap.
Stop admitting new sequence positions at a fixed boundary.
The window is a range of Data sequence numbers for ONE stream direction.
Base = first chunk not yet admitted to the ordered receive buffer.
As contiguous chunks enter that buffer, the base advances and opens new positions.
12 — ACKs tell the sender where the window stands
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / RECEIVE WINDOW · FEEDBACK
ACKs tell the sender where the window stands
The receiver sends a snapshot of its receive window state via ACK frames.
Bitmap bit i describes sequence receiveBase + i.
Sequences below it entered the ordered buffer.
Bits that are set acknowledge chunks even beyond a gap.
ACKs are triggered by accepted Data, duplicates, and receive-base advancement.
One ACK can report several received chunks and window advances.
Width is fixed at 256; the sender derives the limit from the base.
16 — How does A know which SURBs B needs?
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / SUPPLY SNAPSHOT · PURPOSE
How does A know which SURBs B needs?
A supplies SURBs; B reports which arrived and how far A may extend the numbered supply.
First supply sequence not yet received.
All lower sequence numbers are acknowledged.
256 bits for sequences starting at the base.
Bits that are set acknowledge arrivals beyond a missing SURB.
New SURBs must have sequence numbers BELOW this limit.
Removing SURBs from B's queue opens space and raises it.
Initial limit = queue capacity. Taking one SURB for sending increases it by 1.
Receiving SURBs does not change the limit.
17 — When does B send a supply snapshot?
HOW MIXTRANSPORT WORKS / SUPPLY SNAPSHOT · TIMING
When does B send a supply snapshot?
The snapshot accompanies reverse traffic; silence is handled by an explicit status probe.
Data, Ack and other reverse stream/control frames
B takes SURBs out of its queue before reporting the new limit in the outgoing frame.
Receiving SurbSupply alone does not trigger a standalone supply-status reply.
